extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers, students and scholars of biology/natural philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of the general, universal principles (laws) of development and function in organisms as presented in a 19th-century treatise on 'Transcendental Physiology' (laws about growth, heredity, reproduction, differentiation/integration, and the social analogues of biological progress).

rubrics_metrics.name: Development varies as function
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a law of organized bodies that, other things equal, development varies as function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated applicability: not only bones, muscles, nerves, organs of sense, and glands, but 'every gland, every viscus, every element of the body' and even 'a mental faculty.' Qualification: holds provided the performance of function is not so excessive as to produce disorder or exceed the repairing powers of the system or the agencies supplying nutriment. 'On this law are based all maxims and methods of right education, intellectual, moral, and physical.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Hereditary transmission (like produces like)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each plant or animal produces others of like kind: the likeness of kind consists chiefly in assuming the same general structure rather than repeating individual traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers ordinary reappearance of family peculiarities and the origin of permanent varieties (new breeds, races, cultivars). The law is presented as universal across genera, orders, classes and kingdoms. Apparent exceptions (e.g., alternate generation) are noted but treated as probably not true counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fertilized germ as universal starting-point
rubrics_metrics.description: The starting-point of every higher animal or plant, and of clans of organisms propagated by fission or gemmation, is always a spore, seed, or ovum; this fertilized germ results from the union of the contents of two cells.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes universality from infusoria and algae to mammals: even where later multiplication occurs by fission or gemmation, the primary origin is a fertilized germ. Aphis cases and similar experiments are discussed as possible special conditions, but no undoubted exceptions are accepted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progress from the homogeneous to the heterogeneous
rubrics_metrics.description: Every kind of progress is from the homogeneous to the heterogeneous; organisms and systems commence as relatively homogeneous masses and advance toward greater heterogeneity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied not only to individual embryonic development (germ → complex organism) but analogically to language, arts, society, technology. The principle underlies many historical and social examples: differentiation of occupations, effects of inventions (bronze, steam, telegraph) producing multiple secondary changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: One cause produces many effects (decomposition of force)
rubrics_metrics.description: A single cause often produces not only a first dual effect but a number of secondary dual effects; the decomposition of every expended force into several forces perpetually produces higher complication and multiplied results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by economic and technological examples: bronze substituting stone creates new occupations and modifies many crafts; the locomotive/steam-power sets off complex chains of provisional arrangements, trades, transport, social habits and further manufactures. Used to explain why a cause yields manifold and ramified changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Development proceeds by differentiations and integrations
rubrics_metrics.description: The transition from the homogeneous to the heterogeneous is carried on by differentiations and accompanying integrations (not by differentiation alone).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: organs both separate and coalesce in development (heart twisting into a single organ, bile-cells consolidating into liver). The current statement attributing progress to differentiations alone is considered incomplete; integration (coalescence, aggregation) is an essential complementary process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longitudinal integration
rubrics_metrics.description: A mode of integration in development where many serial segments or elements fuse/shorten into fewer consolidated regions along the length of the body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: reduction of segment number from lower to higher Annulosa (worms → insects → crabs), consolidation of embryonic divisions into a compact thorax in crustaceans and insects, fusion of vertebral elements into skull and sacrum, formation of os coccygis by fused caudal vertebrae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transverse integration
rubrics_metrics.description: A mode of integration where paired or lateral structures coalesce or become united across the body axis, producing unification of previously separate elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: double chains of ganglia in lower annulosa becoming a single chain in advanced forms (crayfish ganglia coalescing into brain), convergence and coalescence of oviducts/uteri in mammals, increasing commissural connection of cerebral hemispheres. Detailed serial coalescence patterns are given (e.g., anterior ganglia forming brain).

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration depends on community of function
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrations (coalescences) tend to occur among parts that share or jointly perform common functions; parts performing similar duties tend toward unification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/meanings: fused skull bones protect the cephalic ganglion and provide fulcrum for jaws; pelvic fusion transfers weight to legs; fusion of tibia/fibula and radius/ulna in ungulates relates to habitual limb usage. Modes leading to integration include growth-driven contact, approximation prior to union, or dominance of one organ with others shrinking away.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limiting conditions on integration
rubrics_metrics.description: The tendency to integration acts under limiting conditions which explain apparent exceptions to general integration trends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges that integration is not absolute; the human foetus and lower vertebrata retain certain separations; degrees of coalescence vary across taxa. Recognition of limits clarifies why some lateral organs remain distinct in certain mammalian orders while others coalesce into a single structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population pressure and specialization in societies
rubrics_metrics.description: In social/ economic contexts, increased population and demand force individuals to confine themselves to what they do best, intensifying specialization and producing new occupations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: barter and exchange lead to specialization among tribe members; introduction of new materials (bronze) creates specialized trades; steam-power and railways multiply occupations, modify trade, lower prices, extend travel, and alter habits — illustrating the biological-style law applied to social progress (homogeneous → heterogeneous).
